title: Uncertainties and errors
summary: Every measurement has an [[uncertainty|uncertainty]]. You record it, carry it through calculations and quote results to sensible [[significant-figures|significant figures]]. [[random-error|Random]] and [[systematic-error|systematic errors]] affect [[precision|precision]] and [[accuracy|accuracy]] differently, and [[percentage-error|percentage error]] shows whether a result agrees with an accepted value.

goals.text: Tell random from systematic errors, and say how each affects precision and accuracy.
Round values to a sensible number of significant figures or decimal places.
Record a reading with its [[absolute-uncertainty|absolute uncertainty]], such as $(0.34 \pm 0.01)$ A.
Find [[fractional-uncertainty|fractional]] and [[percentage-uncertainty|percentage uncertainty]] and percentage error, and judge whether a result agrees with an accepted value.
Work out and interpret [[percentage-change|percentage change]] and [[percentage-difference|percentage difference]].
[[propagation-of-uncertainty|Propagate uncertainties]] through sums, differences, products, quotients and powers.

before.prompt: Find the mean of $4.2$, $4.7$ and $4.5$. Give 2 decimal places.
before.hint: Add the values, then divide by how many there are.

before.prompt: A $\pu{60 g}$ sample loses $\pu{9 g}$ of its mass. What percentage of its mass did it lose?
before.hint: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100.
Count from the first non-zero digit.

blocks.text: Time the same event five times and you get five slightly different readings. Errors come in two kinds.

blocks.statement: An error that makes repeated readings scatter unpredictably above and below the true value.
blocks.plain: Readings wobble by a different amount each time.

blocks.statement: An error that shifts every reading in the same direction, by the same amount or fraction.
blocks.plain: Readings are all off in the same way.

blocks.text: Random errors come from things you can't control exactly, like reaction time. Systematic errors come from the instrument or method, like a zero error or heat lost in every trial.

blocks.statement: How close repeated measurements of the same quantity are to each other.
How close a measurement, or the mean of several, is to the true value.
blocks.plain: Accurate readings are centred on the right answer.

blocks.statement: Random errors reduce precision; repeating and averaging reduces their effect. Systematic errors reduce accuracy; repeating does not help, so correct the readings or change the method.
blocks.why: Random errors push readings up as often as down, so they partly cancel in a mean. A systematic error pushes every reading the same way.

blocks.alt: Four rows of five measurement dots, each on its own horizontal line, with a dashed vertical line marking the true value through all four rows. Row 1, precise and accurate: the dots are tightly bunched on the true value. Row 2, precise but not accurate, labelled systematic error: the dots are tightly bunched but all well to the right of the true value. Row 3, accurate but not precise, labelled random error: the dots are widely spread, but centred on the true value. Row 4, neither, labelled both kinds of error: the dots are widely spread and centred well to the right of the true value.
blocks.caption: Precision is the spread of the dots. Accuracy is where their centre sits.

blocks.question: A newton-meter reads $\pu{0.3 N}$ with nothing hanging from it. A student hangs a stone from it three times and records $\pu{4.6 N}$, $\pu{4.7 N}$ and $\pu{4.6 N}$. Explain whether the readings are precise and accurate, and how to correct them.
steps: Marking point 1: the readings agree within $\pu{0.1 N}$: precise.
Marking point 2: every reading is $\pu{0.3 N}$ high: systematic, so not accurate.
Marking point 3: subtract the zero reading: $4.63 - 0.3 \approx \pu{4.3 N}$.
blocks.answer: The readings agree within 0.1 N, so they are precise. The zero error adds 0.3 N to every reading: a systematic error, so they are not accurate. Repeating does not reduce it. Subtract 0.3 N from each reading, or reset the meter to zero, giving about 4.3 N.

verify.truth: precise (readings close); zero error is systematic, so not accurate; repeats don't help; subtract the zero reading

blocks.question: A student times a toy car over a marked distance with a hand-held stopwatch. Five trials give times from $\pu{1.38 s}$ to $\pu{1.71 s}$. Explain the main cause of the spread and how to get a more reliable time.
steps: Marking point 1: varying reaction time is a random error.
Marking point 2: averaging repeats lets the errors partly cancel.
Marking point 3: light gates remove reaction time.
blocks.answer: Reaction time in starting and stopping the watch varies between trials. This random error makes the readings scatter above and below the true time. More repeats and a mean help, because random errors partly cancel. Light gates would remove reaction time altogether.

verify.truth: varying reaction time is a random error; scatter; repeat and average so errors cancel; light gates remove it

blocks.text: Saying repeats make a result more accurate. Averaging reduces random error, which improves precision. A systematic error stays.

blocks.prompt: A metre rule has lost the first $\pu{2 mm}$ of its end. Measuring from that end causes:
blocks.hint: Is every reading off by the same amount, the same way?
blocks.explain: Every length reads $\pu{2 mm}$ too long: precise, perhaps, but off target.

blocks.prompt: Which of these reduces the effect of random errors on a result?
blocks.hint: Which helps errors that go both ways to cancel?
blocks.explain: Random errors partly cancel in a mean. Subtracting a zero reading and recalibrating correct systematic errors, and using one instrument does neither.

blocks.text: $\pu{2.50 m}$ says more than $\pu{2.5 m}$: the final zero shows the length was measured to the nearest centimetre. Digits that carry this information are [[significant-figures|significant figures]].

blocks.statement: The digits of a number that carry meaning about its size and precision, counted from the first non-zero digit.
blocks.plain: The digits you actually measured, with nothing invented.

blocks.text: Non-zero digits always count, and so do zeros between them: $\pu{1.05 kg}$ has three. Leading zeros never count: $\pu{0.0062 m}$ has two.
Trailing zeros count after a decimal point: $\pu{3.40 s}$ has three. In a whole number they are unclear, so write $\pu{1.3e3 m}$ or $\pu{1.30e3 m}$, not $\pu{1300 m}$.

blocks.statement: Multiplying or dividing: give the answer to the fewest significant figures in the data. Adding or subtracting: give it to the fewest decimal places.
blocks.why: A result can't be more precise than the roughest measurement that went into it.

blocks.text: Round only the final answer, never along the way.

blocks.question: A toy car travels $\pu{2.65 m}$ in $\pu{1.8 s}$. Calculate its average speed to an appropriate number of significant figures.
steps: A division: $2.65$ has three significant figures and $1.8$ has two, so give two.

blocks.question: Two resistors are connected in series. One is labelled $22.4\ \Omega$ and the other is measured as $3.87\ \Omega$. Calculate the total resistance to an appropriate precision.
steps: In series, resistances add: $R = 22.4 + 3.87 = 26.27\ \Omega$.
An addition: $22.4$ has one decimal place and $3.87$ has two, so give one.

blocks.prompt: How many significant figures are there in $\pu{0.04070 m}$?
blocks.hint: Leading zeros don't count. A zero at the end of a decimal does.
blocks.explain: The leading zeros don't count; $4$, $0$, $7$ and the final $0$ do.

blocks.prompt: A trolley of mass $\pu{0.250 kg}$ accelerates at $\pu{3.6 m s-2}$. Use $F = ma$ to find the resultant force, in N, to an appropriate number of significant figures.
blocks.hint: A multiplication: count the significant figures in each value.
blocks.explain: $F = 0.250 \times 3.6 = \pu{0.90 N}$: two significant figures, like $3.6$, so keep the final zero.

sections.heading: Recording a measurement with its uncertainty

blocks.text: No instrument gives the exact true value, so every reading comes with an [[uncertainty|uncertainty]].

blocks.statement: The range, above and below a measured value, within which the true value is expected to lie.
blocks.plain: How far off the reading could be, either way.

blocks.statement: The uncertainty in a quantity, given in the same unit as the quantity.
blocks.plain: The plus-or-minus part of a reading, with its unit.

blocks.text: Write value $\pm$ absolute uncertainty, with the unit: $(0.34 \pm 0.01)$ A, or $I = 0.34 \pm \pu{0.01 A}$. The current lies between $\pu{0.33 A}$ and $\pu{0.35 A}$.
1. Analogue scale: half the smallest division, unless the reading is harder to judge.
2. Digital display: one unit in the last digit. A balance showing $\pu{12.47 g}$ has an uncertainty of $\pm\pu{0.01 g}$.
3. Repeated readings: half the range, $\frac{\text{largest} - \text{smallest}}{2}$, if that is bigger than the instrument's uncertainty.

blocks.statement: Round an absolute uncertainty to one significant figure. Then round the value to end at the same decimal place.
blocks.why: The uncertainty shows which decimal place is already in doubt. Digits beyond it carry no information.

blocks.question: An analogue ammeter scale is marked every $\pu{0.02 A}$. The needle points exactly at the $\pu{0.34 A}$ mark. Record the current with its absolute uncertainty.
steps: Analogue scale, so take half the smallest division: $\frac{0.02}{2} = \pu{0.01 A}$.
The uncertainty is in the second decimal place, and so is the reading, so no rounding is needed.

blocks.question: A student times a ball rolling down a ramp five times, with a stopwatch that reads to $\pu{0.01 s}$: $\pu{2.43 s}$, $\pu{2.38 s}$, $\pu{2.46 s}$, $\pu{2.40 s}$ and $\pu{2.44 s}$. Record the mean time with its absolute uncertainty.
steps: Half the range: $\frac{2.46 - 2.38}{2} = \pu{0.04 s}$. It is bigger than the stopwatch's $\pu{0.01 s}$, so use it.
Round the mean to the second decimal place, like the uncertainty.

blocks.prompt: A digital voltmeter displays $\pu{3.07 V}$. What is the absolute uncertainty in this reading?
blocks.hint: For a digital display, look at the last digit.
blocks.explain: One unit in the last digit: $\pm\pu{0.01 V}$. Halving is for analogue scales.

blocks.prompt: A mean length is $\pu{15.264 cm}$, with an absolute uncertainty of $\pu{0.03 cm}$. How should it be recorded?
blocks.hint: Where does the uncertainty's one significant figure sit?
blocks.explain: The uncertainty is in the second decimal place, so the value stops there too.

blocks.text: $\pm\pu{1 mm}$ is tiny on a $\pu{2 m}$ rod but huge on a $\pu{3 mm}$ bead. To compare uncertainties, divide by the value.

blocks.statement: The absolute uncertainty in a quantity divided by its value; also called the relative uncertainty.
blocks.plain: What fraction of the reading is in doubt.
The doubt as a percentage of the reading.

blocks.text: $\Delta x$ is the absolute uncertainty in $x$. Fractional and percentage uncertainties have no unit; give them to one or two significant figures.

blocks.question: A micrometer gives the diameter of a wire as $0.48 \pm \pu{0.01 mm}$. Calculate the fractional and percentage uncertainties in the diameter.
steps: Fractional: $\frac{0.01}{0.48} = 0.0208\ldots \approx 0.021$, with no unit.
Percentage: $0.0208\ldots \times 100\% = 2.08\ldots\%$, to two significant figures.

blocks.text: For the same absolute uncertainty, small readings have large percentage uncertainties. To shrink one, measure something bigger: time ten swings instead of one, or measure a stack of 50 sheets and divide by 50.

blocks.statement: The difference between an experimental value and the accepted value, as a percentage of the accepted value.
blocks.plain: How far your result is from the accepted value, in percent.

blocks.statement: A result agrees with the accepted value if that value lies inside its range (value $\pm$ absolute uncertainty). If it lies outside, or the percentage error is larger than the percentage uncertainty, a systematic error is likely.
blocks.why: The range is where random scatter could put the result. Missing the accepted value by more than that means something pushed it one way.

blocks.alt: A horizontal number line for g in metres per second squared, marked from 9.0 to 10.0 in steps of 0.1. A dot at 9.4 shows the measured value, with a horizontal bar from 9.1 to 9.7 showing its range. A separate vertical marker at 9.81 shows the accepted value. The accepted value lies to the right of the end of the bar, outside the range.
blocks.caption: The range $9.4 \pm 0.3$ runs from $9.1$ to $9.7$. The accepted value, $9.81$, is outside it.

blocks.question: A student drops a ball through light gates and finds $g = 9.4 \pm \pu{0.3 m s-2}$. The accepted value where the student lives is $\pu{9.81 m s-2}$. Comment on whether the result agrees with it, and what this suggests.
steps: Marking point 1: the range is $9.1$ to $\pu{9.7 m s-2}$, and $9.81$ lies outside it.
Marking point 2: percentage error $\frac{0.41}{9.81} \times 100\% \approx 4.2\%$; percentage uncertainty $\frac{0.3}{9.4} \times 100\% \approx 3.2\%$.
Marking point 3: so a systematic error is likely; air resistance would make every value too small.
blocks.answer: The range is 9.1 to 9.7 m s⁻² and the accepted value lies outside it, so the result does not agree. The percentage error, 4.2%, is larger than the percentage uncertainty, 3.2%. So random errors alone cannot explain the gap: a systematic error, such as air resistance, is likely.

verify.truth: accepted value outside 9.1-9.7 range; % error 4.2 > % uncertainty 3.2; systematic error likely (e.g. air resistance)

blocks.prompt: A time is measured as $0.84 \pm \pu{0.02 s}$. What is its percentage uncertainty? Give 2 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Divide the uncertainty by the value, then multiply by 100.

blocks.prompt: A student uses LEDs to find the Planck constant as $\pu{7.1e-34 J s}$. What is the percentage error, compared with the data-booklet value?
blocks.hint: The data booklet gives $h = \pu{6.63e-34 J s}$. Which value goes on the bottom?
blocks.explain: Constants a question doesn't give come from the data booklet. $\frac{7.1 - 6.63}{6.63} \times 100\% = 7.08\ldots\%$.

blocks.text: Two more percentages compare values, not uncertainties. Which one you use depends on whether one value came first.

blocks.statement: The change in a quantity divided by its original value, multiplied by 100%.
blocks.plain: How much something grew or shrank, compared with where it started.

blocks.text: A rise gives a positive percentage change and a fall a negative one. Keep the sign.

blocks.question: When a thermistor is warmed, its resistance falls from $2.40\ \text{k}\Omega$ to $1.65\ \text{k}\Omega$. Calculate the percentage change in its resistance.
steps: Change: $1.65 - 2.40 = -0.75\ \text{k}\Omega$. It is a fall, so it is negative.
Divide by the original: $\frac{-0.75}{2.40} \times 100\% = -31.25\%$. The change $0.75$ has two significant figures, so give two.
The resistance fell by just under a third.

blocks.statement: The difference between two values divided by their mean, multiplied by 100%.
blocks.plain: How far apart two results are, compared with their average.

blocks.text: Use percentage difference when neither value is the right one or the starting one, such as two groups' results. With an accepted value, use percentage error.

blocks.question: Two groups measure the speed of water waves in the same ripple tank: $\pu{1.46 m s-1}$ and $\pu{1.52 m s-1}$. Calculate the percentage difference between their results.
steps: $\frac{0.06}{1.49} \times 100\% = 4.02\ldots\%$. The difference $0.06$ has one significant figure, so give one.
Whether 4% matters depends on each group's percentage uncertainty.

blocks.prompt: A solar panel's output rises from $\pu{250 W}$ to $\pu{320 W}$ after cleaning. What is the percentage change? Give 2 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Divide the change by the original value.
blocks.explain: $\frac{320 - 250}{250} \times 100\% = +28\%$, positive because it is a rise.

blocks.prompt: Two students find the same spring constant by different methods. There is no accepted value. Which quantity best compares their results?
blocks.hint: Neither result came first, and neither is known to be right.
blocks.explain: Percentage error needs an accepted value, and percentage change needs an original value.

blocks.text: Most results are calculated from several measurements, each with its own uncertainty. [[propagation-of-uncertainty|Propagation of uncertainty]] combines them into the uncertainty of the result.

blocks.statement: Working out the uncertainty in a calculated result from the uncertainties in the quantities used to calculate it.
blocks.plain: Passing the doubt in your readings on to your answer.

blocks.text: Three rules cover every case. They are printed in the data booklet under Uncertainties, so the skill is choosing the right one.

blocks.tex: y = a \pm b \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta y = \Delta a + \Delta b

blocks.text: 1. Adding or subtracting: add the absolute uncertainties, even for a subtraction. They never cancel.
2. Multiplying or dividing: add the fractional (or percentage) uncertainties, then multiply by $y$ for the absolute uncertainty.
3. Raising to a power: multiply the fractional uncertainty by the size of the power. A square root, power $\tfrac12$, halves it.
Exact numbers, such as the $\tfrac12$ in $\tfrac12 mv^{2}$ or the $2$ and $\pi$ in $2\pi r$, have no uncertainty.

blocks.question: The potential difference across a resistor is $4.5 \pm \pu{0.1 V}$ and the current is $0.30 \pm \pu{0.01 A}$. Determine its resistance, $R = \frac{V}{I}$, with its absolute uncertainty.
steps: Value: $R = \frac{4.5}{0.30} = 15\ \Omega$.
Dividing, so add fractional uncertainties: $\frac{0.1}{4.5} + \frac{0.01}{0.30} = 0.0222\ldots + 0.0333\ldots = 0.0555\ldots$
$\Delta R = 0.0555\ldots \times 15 = 0.833\ldots\ \Omega \approx 0.8\ \Omega$, to one significant figure.
That is the first decimal place, so give $R$ as $15.0\ \Omega$. With an uncertainty, it sets the decimal places, not the significant-figure rule.

blocks.question: A trolley of mass $0.600 \pm \pu{0.006 kg}$ moves at $2.5 \pm \pu{0.1 m s-1}$. Determine its kinetic energy, $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^{2}$, with its absolute uncertainty.
steps: Value: $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 \times 0.600 \times 2.5^{2} = \pu{1.875 J}$.
Fractional uncertainties: mass $\frac{0.006}{0.600} = 0.01$; speed $\frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.04$, doubled because $v$ is squared: $0.08$. The $\tfrac12$ adds nothing.
Total $0.09$, so $\Delta E_\text{k} = 0.09 \times 1.875 = 0.16875 \approx \pu{0.2 J}$.
Round the value to the first decimal place: $\pu{1.9 J}$.

blocks.text: Adding absolute uncertainties in a product or quotient. Their units often don't even match. Add fractional uncertainties, then convert back.
In Paper 1A, propagation questions are quickest in percentages: add them for products and quotients, and multiply by the power.

blocks.prompt: A spring is $12.7 \pm \pu{0.1 cm}$ long unloaded and $18.4 \pm \pu{0.1 cm}$ long with a load. What is its extension?
blocks.hint: A subtraction: what happens to the absolute uncertainties?
blocks.explain: $18.4 - 12.7 = \pu{5.7 cm}$; the uncertainties add to $\pu{0.2 cm}$. That is 3.5%, against under 1% per length: subtracting close values inflates it.

blocks.prompt: Radiated power is proportional to $T^{4}$, with $T$ in kelvin. If $T$ has a percentage uncertainty of $1.5\%$, what is the percentage uncertainty in the power?
blocks.hint: A power of 4 multiplies the percentage uncertainty by 4.

blocks.text: Random error: scatter, lowers precision, reduced by averaging repeats. Systematic error: same shift each time, lowers accuracy, not reduced by repeats.
$\times$ and $\div$: fewest significant figures. $+$ and $-$: fewest decimal places.
Analogue: half the smallest division. Digital: one unit in the last digit. Repeats: half the range. Uncertainty to 1 s.f., value to the same decimal place.
Percentage change $= \frac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%$. Percentage difference $= \frac{\lvert a - b \rvert}{\text{mean}} \times 100\%$.
Sums and differences: add absolute uncertainties. Products and quotients: add fractional ones. Power $n$: multiply by $\lvert n \rvert$.
Accepted value outside the range, or percentage error above percentage uncertainty: a systematic error is likely.

mistakes: Writing 'human error' or 'to reduce error'. Name the error as random or systematic, give its cause, and say what your change does to it.
Quoting too many digits, such as $15 \pm 0.833\ \Omega$. Round the uncertainty to one significant figure, then match the value: $15.0 \pm 0.8\ \Omega$.
Subtracting uncertainties when values are subtracted. Absolute uncertainties always add.
Forgetting the power. In $v^{2}$ the fractional uncertainty in $v$ counts twice; an exact $\tfrac12$ or $\pi$ adds nothing.
Dividing by your own result in a percentage error. Divide by the accepted value.
Calling a result correct because its percentage error is small. It agrees only if the accepted value lies inside its range.
examTips: 'Determine the absolute uncertainty' needs working: the fractional uncertainties, their sum, then multiplying by the value.
To 'state' a result to the appropriate precision, give the uncertainty to one significant figure, match the value's decimal places, and add the unit.
To 'comment on' agreement with an accepted value, give the range, say whether the accepted value is inside it, and if not name a likely systematic error. Paper 1B data-based questions test this.
